title: Equatorward upper-ocean heat transport from the Southern Ocean boosted interglacial warming

paper_content.abstract: The Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT) signifies a pivotal shift in glacial–interglacial cycles with intensified interglacial warming, yet its underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Targeting the most sensitive component of oceanic heat uptake, the southern-sourced sub-surface waters, the post-MBT ocean heat dynamics are investigated using reconstructed deep and bottom thermocline temperatures from the Western Equatorial Pacific. Our results show that, since the MBT, the deep thermocline temperature has been gradually declining in association with cooling within the (sub)tropical Pacific upper ocean circulation. In contrast, the bottom thermocline temperature shows a pronounced rising trend independent of the calibration-derived uncertainties in its absolute estimates. Such post-MBT bottom thermocline warming is consistent with an enhanced advection of southern-sourced subsurface waters, as indicated by strengthened Southern Ocean meridional thermal gradients and concurrent warming in the southern subtropics. It is thus suggested that enhanced equatorward transport of southern-sourced subsurface waters, as a cross-hemispheric heat-redistribution pathway, may have elevated the background thermal state of post-MBT interglacials, highlighting the potential role of tropical-Southern Ocean connection in shaping climate trajectories.
paper_content.introduction:
The ocean stores more than 90% of the excess heat from anthropogenic forcing, making it the dominant reservoir of the present energy imbalance1–3. The way of the heat being partitioned within the thermocline and intermediate layers of the ocean influences energy exchange between hemispheres and hence climate feedbacks in modern days4–6, while paleo records show that meridional heat transport between the poles and the equator has influenced climate sensitivity on orbital to millennial timescales7–9. At the center of ocean heat redistribution is the Southern Ocean10–12, where formation and subduction of the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) and Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) ventilate the ocean interior with varying heat, carbon, and nutrients13–15. These water masses connect high-latitude surface forcing to low-latitude upper-ocean ventilation. Their past variability therefore provides key constraints on how ocean heat redistribution has shaped long-term climate transitions.

Modern observations highlight the importance of mode and intermediate waters in global heat uptake and reveal a strong hemispheric asymmetry3,16, with most ocean heat gain occurring in the Southern Hemisphere5. Yet instrumental records are too short to resolve their role over large-amplitude climate shifts. The Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT), occurring around ~430 thousand-years ago (ka), marks a fundamental shift toward warmer interglacials with higher atmospheric CO2, such as during the Holocene17,18. Although the MBT is not a direct analogue for modern warming, it provides a process-based reference for examining how internal reorganization of the climate system amplified interglacial warmth within the range of natural boundary conditions in the Quaternary (Figs. 1a, d, e). Given the relatively consistent orbital configurations over the past million years20, warmer interglacials after the MBT (post-MBT; ~430 ka onward) are generally attributed to stronger internal feedbacks than those before the MBT (~800–430 ka)19 (Figs. 1d, e), especially the processes of heat distribution within the ocean-atmosphere system.

Upper-ocean heat storage in the Pacific, shaped by wind-driven subtropical cells and thermocline dynamics, regulates the distribution of heat and moisture across the ocean-atmosphere system, thereby influencing global climate variability4,21,22. The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP) is a key region where the upper-ocean heat, coupling with intense atmospheric convection, modulates the ocean-atmosphere moisture budget on orbital time-scales8,23–25. Given such importance, the upper-ocean heat dynamics across the (sub)tropical Pacific is supposed to contribute to the post-MBT climate amplification. Previous studies have paid greater attention to deep-ocean ventilation26 and carbon cycling27, whereas the role of upper- to intermediate-ocean heat transport has been less explored. However, direct evidence linking variability in SAMW and AAIW formation to equatorward heat transport on orbital timescales remains limited.

Here we examine the changes in upper- to intermediate-ocean circulation through MBT, particularly involving SAMW and AAIW, to assess the associated effect of equatorward heat transport for post-MBT interglacial warming. To test this hypothesis, we reconstructed deep- and bottom-thermocline water temperatures (DTT and BTT, respectively) from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U148928 (2°07.19’N, 141°01.67’E, water depth 3421 m), located at the center of the IPWP, spanning the past ~670 kyr (Figs. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1a). The reconstructions are derived from Mg/Ca ratios of two planktonic foraminiferal species, Globorotalia tumida and Globorotalia crassaformis, which calcify at ~200 m (i.e., deep thermocline) and ~330–600 m (i.e., bottom thermocline)29–32, respectively (see Methods and Supplementary Material 1). Since available Mg/Ca-temperature calibrations for G. crassaformis were developed from Atlantic Ocean, all reported temperature variations focus on their relative variations and long-term trends that are little affected by the choice of calibrations32 (detailed in Supplementary Materials 1–3). The BTT variations are emphasized because of its direct linkage to the penetration depth and thermohaline properties of SAMW and AAIW, while the DTT record is used alongside to illustrate the thermocline dynamics across the MBT. By linking these changes in IPWP thermocline structure to southern-sourced intermediate-water circulation, we identified a mechanism of equatorward heat redistribution with implications for interglacial climate evolution.
paper_content.results:
Divergent deep and bottom thermocline changes

The DTT record of Site U1489 documents significant cycles with dominant 100-kyr and 23-kyr periodicities (above 90% confidence interval, Supplementary Figs. 2a, c), showing warmer values aligned with precession minima, especially during interglacial peaks (e.g., peaks at Marine Isotope Stages (MIS) 5, 9, 13, and 15; Figs. 1d, 2a; Supplementary Material 4). These patterns match with the shallower thermocline water temperature records from the IPWP and indicate a common modulation of precession-paced inter-hemispheric summer insolation gradient on the Pacific Subtropical Cells (STCs)8,21. Our results reaffirm a similar precession-driven STCs mechanism governing the thermal condition throughout the shallow to deep waters within the IPWP thermocline.

The mean values of our DTT show a slight cooling trend by ~0.9℃±0.2 ℃ (1σ, from 18.6 ℃ to 17.7 ℃) starting from ~470 ka, around the boundary between MIS 13 and 12 (Fig. 1b). This DTT cooling exhibits correspondence with the sea surface temperature (SST) trends in the center of the IPWP33,34 (Supplementary Figs. 3a, b) and with thermocline water temperature reconstructions across the western and eastern equatorial Pacific, pointing to a basin-wide shoaling and cooling of the tropical Pacific thermocline across the Pleistocene35,36(Supplementary Figs. 3c, d). Such changes were likely mediated by variations in the Equatorial Undercurrent and upwelling dynamics37,38.

The DTT cooling is further corroborated by a weak cooling trend in the mid-latitude North Pacific39, and a southward migration of both the Northern Hemisphere westerlies and the North Equatorial Counter Current during the same interval40,41(Figs. 2c, d), thus indicating a cooling and equatorward contraction of Pacific STCs (Fig. 2e). The associated cooling trend in the subtropical North Pacific would enhance thermocline ventilation along isopycnals21,42, thereby facilitating subduction of subtropical cold anomalies into the tropical upper-waters. Both modeling and observational studies indicate that temperature anomalies originating from the subtropics are transmitted equatorward to imprint on the equatorial thermocline, through pathways in the interior and western boundary of Pacific43,44. These lines of evidence allow us to attribute the long-term deep thermocline cooling in the Western Equatorial Pacific since ~470 ka to an intensified northern-sourced cold-water supply through a contracted STCs system. Independent reconstructions of G. tumida from the eastern tropical Pacific (ODP Site 1236) are consistent with our results and confirm the observed long-term DTT cooling as basin-scale thermocline changes rather than a site-specific feature or ecological artifacts45 (Supplementary Fig. 3e).

Differing from DTT, the BTT is dominated by obliquity cyclicities (41-kyr; Figs. 1c, e and Supplementary Figs. 2b, d), indicating sensitivity of the IPWP bottom thermocline to higher-latitude processes, which are more dominated by obliquity-paced cross-latitude insolation-gradient forcing46. Notably, variations in all the proxy records of G. crassaformis display relatively small amplitudes before MIS13 but enlarged variations after MIS12 (Supplementary Figs. 4e–g). The obliquity signal in BTT also strengthens since 400 ka and may be linked to the post-MBT intensification of obliquity forcing47, indicating an increased influence of higher-latitude processes on BTT variability.

Since the MBT, BTT rose on average by ~1.8±0.1 ℃ (1σ), from its prior-MBT foothold (from ~670 to 470 ka) with smaller-amplitude variations (~1 °C) (Fig. 1c). Sensitivity tests among Mg/Ca-temperature calibrations confirm the increase in G. crassaformis Mg/Ca ratios as the primary origin of such post-MBT BTT warming, and the choice of calibrations merely determines the baseline of absolute temperature estimates (Supplementary Material 3 and Supplementary Table 1). To explain the BTT warming trend since ~470 ka, one might speculate a long-term upward movement of the calcification depth of G. crassaformis. However, the δ13C of G. crassaformis closely parallels that of G. tumida and maintains a consistent offset from shallower-dwelling species (Supplementary Figs. 5a, b and Supplementary Material 4), indicating stable biogeochemical and thermohaline gradients vertically across their habitat depths. The δ18O of G. crassaformis do show a progressive negative shift, but it agrees largely with the BTT warming (Supplementary Figs. 4e, f). Moreover, given the consistent inter-species δ18O gradients from the mixed layer to the deep thermocline across the MBT, the progressive lightening of G. crassaformis δ18O may not be derived from a shoaling of its habitat depth but warming and/or freshening of the water-mass (Supplementary Figs. 5c–e). Collectively, the coherent trends since MIS 13/12 among the δ13C, δ18O, and the Mg/Ca-derived BTT at Site U1489, argue against any progressive habitat-depth shift of G. crassaformis, instead indicating changes in the thermohaline properties of the bottom-thermocline water mass.

Southern origin of the IPWP bottom thermocline warming

The substantial warming of bottom-thermocline waters in the center of the IPWP since ~470 ka (Fig. 3a) may be explained by two orthogonal scenarios: (1) vertically increased mixing from the shallower warmer waters, and (2) advectively from an enhanced equatorward transport of warmer waters via the SAMW and/or AAIW. The first scenario contradicts other proxy reconstructions. If downward mixing had dominated, the δ18O gradient between surface- and thermocline-dwelling foraminiferal species would have diminished. However, δ18O records from G. ruber, P. obliquiloculata, and G. tumida at Site U148948 varied parallel to one another, with little systematic change in the δ18O gradient between mixed layer and deep thermocline since ~670 ka (Supplementary Figs. 5c, e, and Supplementary Material 4). In addition, downward mixing would imply thickened warm-water pile-up in IPWP and thereby enlarged thermal contrast zonally across the tropical Pacific. However, the zonal SST gradient has slightly weakened since MIS12 (Fig. 2f), which conflicts with this scenario. Hence, a downward vertical mixing scenario is not supported by the available proxy evidence.

The second mechanism, advection of southern-sourced waters, is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. An increase of 2–4 ℃ in the SST gradients between the southern Subtropical Front (STF) and Subantarctic Front (SAF) since the MBT (Figs. 3a, c, d, Supplementary Fig. 6) is consistent with a strengthening of Southern Hemisphere westerlies (based on a conceptual estimate, see Supplementary Material 6) and supports a Southern Ocean source for the onset of the BTT warming. Stronger westerlies between the SAF and STF would deepen the mixed layer and enhance the Ekman pumping north of the SAF and thus strengthen the SAMW subduction49. Model experiments further suggest that poleward intensification of westerlies can more than double the rates of SAMW/AAIW subduction50,51. Proxy records from higher latitudes also show stronger subtropical flow of the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC) across the Agulhas Plateau52, an intermediate-water cooling in the southwest Pacific associated with a poleward shift of the ACC53 (Fig. 3e), and intensified deep western boundary currents off New Zealand since ~450 ka54. Taken together, these observations indicate stronger subsurface water export from the sub-Antarctic zone and a more vigorous South Pacific overturning, supporting an intensified AAlW formation in accordance with the observed BTT warming.

After correcting for the temperature and ice-volume effects, the δ18O sw-ice of G. crassaformis still shows a trend toward more negative values (Supplementary Fig. 5d and Supplementary Material 5), likely reflecting an increase in buoyancy in its source water. Concurrently, SST in the southern Subtropical Front region has significantly increased since the MBT46 (Fig. 3c; Supplementary Fig. 7). Similar to modern warming scenarios55–57, warmer and shallower SAMW were likely produced with its subduction zone shifted poleward, due to warming-induced buoyancy increases58,59, thereby facilitating advection of the SAMW/AAIW along isopycnals into the IPWP bottom thermocline under strengthened westerlies. Modern observations also suggest that the equatorward heat transport in associated with Southern Ocean warming60, would be enhanced by intensified zonal flows61 and a deepened mixed layer north of the SAF62. Accordingly, together with an associated strengthening of the upper-layer circulation of the subtropical gyre63, the equatorward advection of the SAMW/AAIW has been further enhanced since the MBT.

It is noted that a “young, high-δ13C” signature in the bottom thermocline, as expected from well-ventilated Southern Ocean–sourced waters, is absent in our G. crassaformis record, largely due to the limitation of this δ13C tracer in this region64,65. This is mainly because, as SAMW and AAIW are transported northward, they experience mixing with subtropical and equatorial water masses64–66, and extensive biogeochemical modifications including remineralization of organic matters and transformations of inorganic carbon species67–70. These processes progressively attenuate the original δ13C signal. Consistent with this interpretation, such an expected “young, high-δ13C” signal can only be detected partially in some benthic δ13C records at mid-latitudes71, and may be further diminished equatorward into the tropical Pacific sub-surface.

In summary, the rise in BTT temperature since the MBT at Site U1489 coincided with SST warming in the Southern Hemisphere STF region and a strengthening of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies (Figs. 3a, c, d), suggesting a linkage to the source of bottom thermocline waters. Based on available evidence, we propose that enhanced subduction of a warmer SAMW, together with intensified AAIW advection and South Pacific overturning, facilitated transport of warmer waters from the subtropical Southern Ocean into the IPWP bottom thermocline.

Equatorward upper-ocean heat transport boosted warmer interglacials

The BTT and DTT records of Site U1489 suggest accelerated upper- to intermediate-ocean circulations towards the equator after the MBT. Consonantly, during the post-MBT interglacials, the southern trade winds may have been weakened, and the southern STF migrated southward, as supported by a warming in the Southern mid-latitudes and a reduced SST gradient between the southern subtropics and the IPWP72(Figs. 3b, c, and Supplementary Fig. 7). Also, an equatorward shift of northern westerly winds41 and a southward displacement of the IPWP since MIS12 (Fig. 3b) has been detected, in concert with our DTT cooling. These together indicate an inter-hemispheric asymmetry in Pacific upper-ocean circulation, which is supposed to have facilitated the heat uptake in southern mid-latitude Pacific, and strengthened the linkage between the IPWP and the Southern Ocean. It leads us to propose an enhanced heat storage in the Mode Waters during the post-MBT interglacial periods, in tandem with the elevated atmospheric pCO2 and orbital insolation heating26,73.

Since the MBT, the difference between our DTT and BTT decreased, while the δ18O sw-ice difference between G. tumida and G. crassaformis at Site U1489 increased (Figs. 4a, b, see Methods). These changes may reflect reduced thermal but enhanced salinity gradients between the two, which is consistent with an intensified AAIW subduction in the Southern Ocean since MIS13/12 (~470 ka) (Fig. 5). The relatively stable global deep-water temperatures74 (Fig. 4e), contrasted with warming in the mid- to high-latitude Southern Hemisphere53,75–79 (Figs. 3c and 4c, d), further support this interpretation. The sub-surface ocean circulation and heat export are often regarded as drivers of decadal variability in modern-climate studies4–6,80, whereas the high-latitude dynamics of AAIW and SRAMW in isolation have been largely examined by palaeoceanographic and observational studies14,81,82. By extending these perspectives from short-term variability to orbital timescales, our records suggest that Southern Ocean forcing operates within a dynamically coupled hemispheric heat-redistribution system, in which subsurface waters of the IPWP transmit high-latitude variability to the tropics. This equatorward subsurface transport increased tropical heat content and elevated the background thermal state, providing a key mechanism that could have contributed to the amplification of interglacial warmth after the MBT.

The proposed feedback that stronger Southern westerly winds intensify upper- to intermediate-ocean circulation and sustain northward ocean heat transport resonates with the observed post-industrial trends such as warming and expansion of subtropical western boundary currents55–57, increased Southern Ocean heat uptake10–12 and the strengthened pole-to-equator heat transport62. These insights provide specific targets for numerical model experiments, particularly sensitivity tests on the subduction rate and equatorward heat transport of SAMW/AAIW under varying climate scenarios. In any case, our findings underscore that Southern Ocean subsurface-water dynamics can effectively absorb the excess heat, and yield cascading effects on the tropical Pacific oceanic heat-structure and global climate state.
paper_content.methods:
Samples and Chronology

The studied cores from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U1489 (02°07.19ʹN, 141°01.67ʹE, 3421 m water depth) were drilled during Expedition 363 on the western slope of the southern Eauripik Rise, within the Caroline Basin north off Papua New Guinea28 (Supplementary Fig. 1a). A total of 332 sediment samples were collected from cores of the site at every ~5 cm interval from the upper 15.31 m core composite depth below seafloor (CCSF), covering the past ~670 kyr with a time resolution of ~2 kyr.

Site U1489 age model follows the published framework based on high-resolution Globigerinoides ruber δ18O48. A preliminary age model and baseline sedimentation rate were first defined using magnetic reversals from Hole D, owing to their consistency in depth scale. We aligned glacial–interglacial boundaries to the LR04 global benthic δ18O stack to define stratigraphic tie points and identify individual glacial cycles. These tie points were then used as age controls for constructing the age–depth model, with linear interpolation applied to all samples between 0 and 15.31 m. The resulting age model yields a relatively stable mean sedimentation rate of 2.1 ± 0.7 cm/kyr (1σ), generally higher during interglacials (1.0–4.0 cm/kyr; Supplementary Fig. 4a).

Subsurface Water Masses

In the western equatorial Pacific, shallow thermocline waters are ventilated from the subtropics through the Pacific Subtropical Cells (STCs)21,45 via the North and South Equatorial Currents83. While the Equatorial Undercurrent transports subsurface waters eastward across the basin, thereby linking hydrographic conditions between the western and eastern Pacific84. For the deeper part of the thermocline, the North Pacific Intermediate Water (NPIW) extends southward to ~8°N but is largely blocked from the equatorial band by the stronger influence of the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW)85. The latter is advected through the Solomon Sea along the north coast of Papua New Guinea and extends to ~15°N86–88, where it dominates the bottom thermocline of the western equatorial Pacific. The Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) forms north of the Subantarctic Front (SAF) by wintertime convection and is subsequently advected into the thermocline of the southern subtropical gyres as a key component of the upper limb of the Pacific overturning circulations14,89,90. The SAMW originates mainly from the east and central South Pacific, where it mixes with surrounding waters during formation and northward transport, often together with the AAIW, before entering the subtropical thermocline91,92 (Supplementary Fig. 1c).

At Site U1489, the Equatorial Pacific Intermediate Waters are mainly influenced by AAIW sourced from the southeast Pacific, with additional contributions from the Coral and Tasman Seas and direct Southern Ocean inflow64,65. These circulation pathways make Site U1489 particularly suitable for reconstructing thermocline- and intermediate-water variations and their associated interactions between high and low latitudes. Consistent with previous studies93,94, the GLODAP δ13C distribution shows that newly subducted AAIWP and SAMW exhibit relatively high δ13C values, reflecting quick ventilations from the air-sea interface95 (Supplementary Fig. 1d). In contrast, the deep and bottom thermocline in the western Pacific warm pool have lower δ13C, indicating the attenuation of source water signals due to addition of respired carbon and mixing with older waters.

Planktonic foraminiferal proxies

The subsurface-dwelling species Globorotalia tumida, which calcifies at ~200 m in the western equatorial Pacific29 (detailed in Supplementary Material 1), is commonly used as an indicator of deep thermocline conditions36,96,97. Globorotalia crassaformis calcifies at ~330–600 m in the tropical ocean30,31, and generally above the intermediate waters across ocean basins30–32, so it has been extensively applied to reconstruct deepest thermocline/intermediate-water properties in both the Pacific and Atlantic since the Pliocene30–32,98. Accordingly, we use G. tumida as a proxy for the deep thermocline and G. crassaformis as a proxy for the bottom thermocline, defined relative to their calcification depths (Supplementary Material 1). Proxy records from these species, together with sea surface temperature anomaly (SSTA) stacks (detailed in Supplementary Material 6), therefore provide a means to examine connections between the Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP), Pacific STCs, and Southern Hemisphere mid-latitude processes mediated by the AAIW and SAMW.

Stable isotope and Mg/Ca-temperature analyses

Between 25 and 30 well-preserved specimens of G. tumida and G. crassaformis were hand-picked from the 355–425 μm and 250–425 μm size fractions for stable isotope and Mg/Ca measurement, respectively. All specimens are well preserved based on scanning electron microscopy examinations (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Material 2).

Stable isotope analyses were conducted on a Finnigan MAT253 mass spectrometer with a Kiel IV carbonate preparation device at State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, following ref. 99. Long-term measurement standard deviation is 0.07‰ for δ18O and 0.05‰ (1σ) for δ13C. Results were calibrated to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) scale using the NBS19 standard. The average sampling resolution is ~2–3 kyr for both isotope and Mg/Ca records.

For Mg/Ca analyses, we used a composite cleaning protocol based on the established procedures100 with steps of silicate removal101 and reductive cleaning102. The protocol included sequential removal of clays, oxidative and reductive cleaning, weak acid leaching, and multiple rinses with ultrapure water to eliminate detrital clays, Fe–Mn oxides, and organic matter. Mg/Ca ratios were measured on an Agilent 5110 inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) at the Marine Elements Analysis Laboratory, Northwest University, China. Instrumental drift and analytical precision were monitored using ECRM 752-159103, analyzed after every 11 samples. Replicate analyses (n = 30) yielded reproducibility of 5.1% for G. tumida and 3.2% for G. crassaformis.

Cleaning effectiveness was assessed by correlations between Mg/Ca and Al/Ca, Fe/Ca, and Mn/Ca ratios (Supplementary Figs. 9a–h). In G. tumida, a weak positive correlation between Mn/Ca and Mg/Ca was detected (R2 = 0.26). In contrast, Mn/Ca and Mg/Ca of G. crassaformis shows a strong correlation (R2=0.74, Supplementary Figs. 9i–n), primarily due to elevated Mn/Ca values after ~270 ka (Supplementary Fig. 9f), with no apparent link to BTT warming. This relationship, consistent with previous reports of Mn–Mg coupling104–106, is attributed to Mn-rich surface coatings. Following ref. 107, a Mn correction (assuming Mg/Mn = 0.2 mmol/mol) was applied.

Because Site U1489 lies at a depth of ~3421 m, both dissolution and Mn-corrections were applied following refs. 107 and 108. The Mg/Ca ratio in G. tumida was then converted to deep thermocline temperature (DTT) using a species-specific calibration for the 355–425 μm size fraction from western equatorial Pacific29 (Mg/Ca = 0.33exp (0.097 × DTT)). This calibration was selected after evaluating results from alternative equations against modern hydrographic data (Supplementary Figs. 1b, 10a, 11a–d; see Supplementary Material 3 for details). For G. crassaformis, specific calibration for the western equatorial Pacific has not been established. The Atlantic-based calibration, Mg/Ca = 0.658exp (0.122 × BTT)32 with corrections for Mn-contamination and dissolution108,109, gives the most reasonable BTT estimates, in terms of the comparable Late-Holocene BTT values with respect to the modern temperatures at 330–600 m depth in the western equatorial Pacific (Supplementary Figs. 1b, S10b, 11e–h). Uncertainties were calculated following ref. 109, yielding mean errors of 1.7 ℃ for DTT and 0.6 ℃ for BTT (1σ), respectively.

Calculation of seawater δ18O

Seawater δ18O (δ18Osw) was calculated using the equation from ref. 110: δ18Osw (VSMOW, ‰) = (T(°C) -16.5+4.8×δ18Ocalcite(VPDB, ‰))/4.8+0.27. The global ice volume effect, as reported by ref. 111 was then removed to obtain δ18Osw-ice, which reflects local/regional freshwater (or salinity) budget. The δ18Osw-ice errors (see ref. 109 for details) are 0.03‰ for G. tumida and 0.10‰ for G. crassaformis (1σ).

Regional SST stacks and gradients

We compiled subsurface/thermocline records from the IODP Site U1489 and SST reconstructions from Western and Eastern Equatorial Pacific, and Southern Ocean frontal zones (STF and SAF). All datasets, proxies (Mg/Ca or alkenone), coordinates, water depths, and references are listed in Supplementary Table 2. For regional stacks, individual series were linearly interpolated to 4-kyr, adjusted by subtracting the maximum value over the entire time window, smoothed with a 20-kyr running mean, and then averaged. When combining Mg/Ca and alkenone, we used anomalies to minimize method-specific offsets (detailed discussion see Supplementary Material 6). Zonal equatorial Pacific SST gradient is calculated by the difference of SST anomaly between western and eastern equatorial Pacific (ΔSSTAW−E = SSSTAMD97-2140 − SSTODP846), and meridional frontal gradient by those between STF and SAF (ΔSSTASTF−SAF = SST stack (STF) − SST stack (SAF); detailed in Supplementary Material 7).

Time series analyses

To evaluate the orbital pacing and long-term trends, all SSTA records shown in the main text were first linearly interpolated at 4-kyr intervals, and then smoothed with a 20-kyr running average after. Records from IODP Site U1489 were processed using a three-point running average and LOESS smoothing with a Gaussian fit (span = 0.5), and then further smoothed with LOESS (smoothing factor = 0.3) to acquire their long-term trends. Spectral analysis was carried out using the REDFIT procedure112 as implemented in PAST v4.03113. Rectangular windows were applied with an oversampling factor of 6, and the data were divided into two equal-length segments to estimate the red-noise spectra. Wavelet analysis of the temperature reconstructions was performed using Acycle v2.8, following standard procedures114. RAMPFIT regressions were applied to identify changing points in long-term trends115.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: Based on high-resolution paleoceanographic reconstructions of deep and bottom thermocline temperatures from Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP) records, Yang et al. investigate the thermal evolution of the upper-to-intermediate ocean equatorial Pacific over the last 700 ka. The central discussion is based on the differences in behavior between two thermocline depths after ~470 ka, where small deep thermocline cooling is concomitant with substantial warming of bottom thermocline temperatures. Authors argue that this warming originates from the Southern Ocean, driven by Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) with intensification of Antarctic Intermediate Water formation. Overall, the paper is really good. Although disagreements among compared records could be better accounted for to avoid simplification of the mechanism, the discussion is well-written and presents a plausible mechanism, is conclusive, providing novel insights into thermal evolution and ocean-atmospheric interactions in the southern Pacific across the Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT). The new dataset is valuable, and, together with the interpretations, it makes a significant contribution to the scientific community. However, there are a few major issues related to the figures and the method description that need attention. Additionally, there are a few major points that need to be improved to adhere to a global framework and to clarify data comparisons with existing published records. As such, I can`t recommend the manuscript for publication in its present form. As detailed below, the authors should provide more clear descriptions of their results when combined with their respective interpretations. Major comments: First, the manuscript would benefit from better-constructed figures and reorganization of its panels. Although all the used records are there and they look very nice, most of the figure citations in the main text refer to figures in the Supplementary Material, which makes it difficult to follow most of the time. For example, Fig. 1 is almost not used and could be replaced. Figure captions require improvement, as they are often too simplistic and fail to describe their purpose clearly. Second, the introduction needs improvement to contextualize the theme in a broader sense. I am also missing previous paleoceanographic reconstructions and background information related to the dynamics of upper-ocean heat content in the region. Initially, I was confused about whether the paper discussion focused on the causes or effects of the MBT, and I think it would be better clarified from the outset, with a closer tie to the latest topic. A lot of the produced records are in the Supplementary Material and haven't been used in their totality and could be further explored. Third, the methods section is a critical point and needs several improvements. Although the age model for IODP Site 1489 had already been published, I missed at least a general overview of how it was built, including the radiocarbon data used, the calibration curve employed, the alignment method, the interpolation method, and the mean sedimentation rate produced. Although the table listing the used sediment cores is presented in the Supplementary Material, it is not described in the methods, which records were used to calculate the temperature gradients. RAMPFIT and spectral analysis were not even mentioned in the methods and need to be described. Took me a lot of time to understand how trends were estimated. The uncertainties are not mentioned in the manuscript text and or presented in figures, which are also provided in the RAMPFIT results and need to be shown. Finally, the quality of the foraminifera Mg/Ca measurements should be accounted for in the Supplementary Material and other Element/Ca ratios presented, such as Al/Ca, Mn/Ca, and Fe/Ca, and by preferentially evaluating the absolute values and correlation against Mg/Ca to evaluate the cleanning efficiency. A brief explanation of the cleaning procedure performed would be helpful, as a reductive step was included, which may impact the results. Error envelopes could be provided on all temperature records, once they were calculated following Mohtadi et al. (2014). Other comments: Lines 88-89: I see the reference, but you didn`t describe how you calculated the SST gradients from Fig. 2, for example. Lines 88-91: I agree that there is an expressive shift from MIS 12/11 towards the present on Fig. 2b. However, it is not necessarily following the long-term trend seen on DTT. Does it mean that other factors might be controlling BTT? Lines 117-127: Two possibilities were raised to explain BTT warming, one of which is related to downward water mass mixing from surface layers toward the bottom thermocline, which was ruled out by the argument that would result in an intensified east-west Pacific temperature gradient. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: General comments The study by Yang and co-authors presents new reconstructions of deep- and bottom-thermocline water temperatures (DTT and BTT, respectively) from IODP Site U1489, located in the centre of the Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP), spanning the past ~670 kyr. These new datasets, combined with previously published records, offer the opportunity to investigate key aspects of ocean-atmosphere interactions across the Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT). Considering that the MBT marks a fundamental reorganisation of glacial–interglacial cycles, characterised by intensified interglacial warming, and that its underlying drivers remain debated, the manuscript addresses a topic of considerable relevance to the scientific community. The authors propose that accelerated upper- to intermediate-ocean circulation in the mid- to low-latitude Pacific may have amplified post-MBT interglacial warming, with the Southern Ocean playing a significant role in shaping these changes. While the manuscript presents valuable new valuable data and addresses an important scientific question, several aspects of the study require clarification and refinement to enhance its scientific rigour and overall readability. In particular, the structure of the introduction would benefit from a more logical progression, beginning with the broader context, followed by knowledge gaps, the working hypothesis, and site justification. Furthermore, some conceptual oversimplifications should be avoided, for example, the direct comparison between the MBT and present-day anthropogenic warming, which is more complex than implied. Methodological details also require improvement, including further details about the species selection, the presentation of the age model, describing the time series analyses, and the description of oceanographic settings. These elements are essential to support interpretations related to regional and large-scale circulation changes. Greater attention to supplementary material, including clearer figure captions, consistent terminology, and acknowledgement of potential methodological limitations (e.g., combining different SST proxies), will strengthen the overall contribution of the study. Finally, while the research addresses a scientifically significant topic and provides valuable new data and insights, the manuscript would benefit from a more in-depth discussion with additional detail regarding the proposed mechanism. Addressing the points outlined below will improve the clarity, methodological robustness, and interpretive strength of the study. Moreover, a more comprehensive comparison with modern oceanographic conditions, as well as the inclusion of paleoclimate modelling to further support the proposed mechanism, would greatly improve the manuscript. Specific comments - Introduction: the introductory text would benefit from a more logical flow and structure. A clearer step-by-step development from global context → knowledge gaps → hypothesis → site justification would enhance readability. Also, the claim that the MBT provides a paleo-analogue for current anthropogenic warming is oversimplified. - Line 71: the calcification depths of the chosen foraminiferal species should be consistent with what is presented in the methods section (lines 218 and 221). - Lines 72–74: at the beginning of this paragraph, you mention that deep- and bottom-thermocline water temperatures were reconstructed from IODP Site U1489. However, in lines 72–74, you state that the focus is on BTT, which sounds somewhat inconsistent. - Lines 80-83: consider showing shallow thermocline records together with your DTT. - Lines 88-90: same as previous comment. Additionally, the authors argue that IPWP DTT and SST show a cooling trend starting around ~470 kyr. The cited publication (i.e. de Garidel-Thoron et al., 2005) actually suggests a long-term stability of western Pacific warm pool SST during the Pleistocene. Check this inconsistency. - Lines 91-92: Regarding the text “The DTT cooling is also corroborated by a similar weak cooling in the mid-latitude North Pacific25 and a strengthening trend of Northern westerly winds26 (Supplementary Fig. 2b, c),”, the mentioned panels of Supplementary Figure 2 indicates a southward shift of the westerlies and not a strengthening. Please, clarify the text to keep consistency. Lines 93-95: provide a reference for this statement. Additionally, this statement could be further detailed, linking the observed cooling to the strength and southward migration of the northern westerlies. Lines 96-103: as far as I can see in Figure 1e, between around 550 and 400 kyr, there is a decoupling between BTT-Band pass filtering and obliquity signal. It should be acknowledged and discussed. - Lines 105–110: The authors state that the G. crassaformis δ¹³C record remains parallel to those of shallower-dwelling species (i.e., G. tumida, G. ruber, and P. obliquiloculata), indicating a persistent ecological gradient throughout the studied interval. While it is evident that δ¹³C records of G. crassaformis and G. tumida follow a parallel trend (with G. crassaformis consistently showing lower δ¹³C values), the δ¹³C records of G. ruber and P. obliquiloculata appear to exhibit similar absolute values to G. crassaformis (around 1‰). How do the authors explain this apparent similarity in δ¹³C values despite the differences in habitat depth among these species? - Lines 120–127: scenario 1 could be more clearly explained in terms of a deepening of the thermocline in the western equatorial Pacific, i.e. intensified trade winds → enhanced east–west transport of warm surface waters → pilling up of warm waters in the western equatorial Pacific -> deepening of the thermocline → DTT warming. - Lines 135-140: to clarify why a strengthening of the SAMW transport cannot account to the observed SAMW warming as well as that a strengthening of the SAMW transport would imprint a positive signature on δ¹³C of bottom thermocline waters in the IPWP, the methods subsection related to modern conditions should include information on the present-day oceanographic settings at both core location and SAMW formation region. - Lines 135-138: An increased export of SAMW wouldn’t be related to a decrease in δ¹³C? - Lines 170-171: Regarding the text “Progressive mid-latitude warming in the Southern Hemisphere”, this warming is proposed considering SST records, right? Please clarify it in the text. - Lines 191-192: Regarding the text “While previous studies focused on high-latitude AAIW dynamics and their role in global heat transport, our study….”, provide reference(s) to this statement. - Methods: much of the interpretation relies on time series analyses (e.g., interpolation, resampling, filtering, running averages, detrending, LOESS regression, spectral analysis, ramp function regression, and so on). It would be interesting to add a “time series” subsection describing each of these techniques within the methodology. If there is no space for it in the main text, it could be inserted in the supplementary information. - Line 207 (Methods subsection “Study site location and sampling”): provide information on the IODP expedition which collected the studied marine core. Additionally, a broad description of the oceanographic setting (specifically the water masses and circulation patterns influencing the study site) is currently missing. This information is crucial to support the discussion, which addresses the influence, for example, of the North Pacific and the Southern Ocean on the study area. Furthermore, the age model for core U1489 requires a more thorough explanation. In particular, the choice of G. ruber over benthic foraminifera should be explained. Providing a supplementary figure illustrating the age model for the target interval is strongly recommended. - Line 216 (subsection “Planktonic foraminiferal ecology and its role in indicating water mass properties”): a more comprehensive description of the planktonic foraminiferal species used in the study is necessary. For example, based on sediment trap studies, is the shell flux to the seafloor seasonal or year-round? Consequently, are the geochemical records derived from these species seasonally biased, or do they reflect annual mean conditions? - Lines 223-227: the sentence “In general, the subsurface-dwelling Pulleniatina obliquiloculata, which calcifies at depths of less than 150 m, is considered an indicator of upper thermocline water properties21,53” seems out of context in this part of the text. - Line 233 (Methods subsection titled “Isotope analysis and Mg/Ca-temperature estimate”): Please (i) provide references related to the species used for the analyses; (ii) include the sampling resolution for both the δ¹⁸O/δ¹³C and Mg/Ca measurements; (iii) specify the carbonate preparation device coupled to the MAT253 mass spectrometer; (iv) be more specific to which Mg/Ca cleaning procedure was implemented and describe any modification if there was one (three slightly different procedures were cited); (v) include information on how potential contamination (e.g. silicates Mn-bearing phases and clay contamination) was assessed in the trace element analyses. - Line 258 (Methods subsection “Calculation of seawater δ¹⁸O”): given the length of the record spanning multiple G-I cycles, the reason for not applying ice volume correction to the δ¹⁸Osw data should be explained. - Line 455 (Figure 2): the caption text related to panel d should specify which cores were used to calculate the anomaly between STF and SAF. Double-check it for all presented figures. - Line 477 (Figure 4): in the section “Divergent deep and bottom thermocline changes”, the authors present and discuss a cooling trend of SST and DTT in the IPWP, starting from at ca. 470 kyr. This cooling trend does not seem to be represented in this figure. - Line 502 (Supplementary Text 1): the residual records should be explained in greater detail, either in the Methods section and/or in Supplementary Information 1. - Lines 512-513: by looking at supplementary Figure 3, it seems that δ¹⁸O-residual from G. crassaformis also exhibits a statistically significant precession signal. Additionally, please double-check Figure 3 regarding the description of the lines indicating the 99% and 95% confidence levels. In the figure itself, these lines are labelled as 90% and 95%, while the caption refers to them as 99% and 95%. - Line 543 (Supplementary text titled “Verification of sea surface temperature stacks”): this section focuses on describing the SSTA stacks. From Supplementary Table 1, it is possible to identify that the records used to construct the SSTA stacks were obtained using two different methods, i.e. Mg/Ca and UK’37. This difference should be acknowledged in the supplementary text, along with a discussion of the potential implications of combining records derived from distinct methods, especially knowing that alkenones and Mg/Ca might show different patterns (e.g. Leduc et al., 2010, 10.1016/j.quascirev.2010.01.004) . - Line 555 (Supplementary figure 1): please clarify in the caption the elements shown in panel b (e.g., white arrow, triangle, foraminifera illustration, selected latitudinal section). - Lines 577: It would be interesting to add in the spectral analysis supplementary figure 3 an evolutionary method (e.g., wavelet analysis) to see whether the identified orbital parameters are constant throughout the record or if there is any change in the dominant cycle that might be related to the findings. Technical corrections - Line 22: “Targeting the most…”. The word “at” is unnecessary here. - Line 48: the acronym MBE was used instead of the already defined MBT. - Line 50: “...for instance, the Holocene”. - Line 50: “…are marked by…”. Use plural once it refers to the interglacials. - Line 51: double-check the cited panels from Figure 1. Maybe, only Fig. 1a would be appropriate to cite here. - Line 52: “...essentially the result of…” instead “...essentially resulted from…” - Line 54: it would be convenient to cite here Fig. 1d, e. - Lines 58 and 559: Homogenise the way you refer to the IPWA, i.e. “Indo-Pacific Warm Pool” or “Indo-Pacific warm pool”. - Line 64: “carbon cycling” instead of “carbon-cycling”. - Line 69: please include a reference to the methods subsection where the study site is described. - Lines 79-80: it would be appropriate to cite also panel d of Figure 1. - Line 103: also cite Figure 1c in this sentence. - Line 107: The word “with” is unnecessary. - Line 113: “...shifting in δ18O of…”. - Line 121: “...were the result of…” instead “...were resulted from…”. - Lines 156-157: “...and warm SAMW would be transported…”. To keep consistent verb tense. - Line 163: “evidences” instead of “evidence”. - Line 179: “contributed” instead of “contribute”. - Line 212: “interval” instead of “intervals”. - Line 230: the acronym SSTA should be presented in full the first time it appears in the text. - Line 256: Delete the word “calculation”. - Line 453: “3-point running average” instead of “3 points running average”. - Line 473: Same as line 455. - Line 511: correct to “~41- and 23-kyr bands”. - Line 536: “...based on of G. tumida…”. Delete the word “of”. - Line 562: “The filed circles…”. Correct to “filled”. - Line 567 (Supplementary Figure 2): I would suggest not invert the y-axis of panel e to facilitate the rationale. - Line 569: Same as line 455. - Line 604: In the sentence “The thin, thin medium, and thick curves…”. You can use just “thin, medium, and thick” instead. - Line 605: Same as line 455. - Line 642: In the supplementary table 1, adjust the first column name to “Region”.

Supplementary Fig. 2e shows that the 151 increased gradient remains high even when the MBT has already occurred. The timing 152 disagreement weakens your argument. If downward mixing is discarded, why did it not 153 follow the same long-term trend and timing as seen on BTT? Adv.), which 166 does not support enhanced downward mixing. 167 Following your suggestion, we plotted δ13C and δ18O of four planktonic foraminiferal 168 species to indicate the upper ocean stratification (Fig. R1and Supplementary Fig. 5 of 169 the revised manuscript), although we did not directly calculate the δ18O gradient 170 between 171 172 Fig. R1 Planktonic isotope records from IODP Site U1489. a δ13C of Globigerinoides ruber (gray) 173 and Pulleniatina obliquiloculata (gold) (Dang et al., 2024); b δ13C of Globorotalia tumida (blue) 174 and Globorotalia crassaformis (red); c δ18O of G. ruber (gray), P. obliquiloculata (gold), G. tumida 175 (blue) and G. crassaformis (red); d δ18O of G. tumida (blue) and G. crassaformis (red); e δ18O 176 gradient between the mixed-layer and thermocline (δ18O (green) and δ18O 177 (blue). ## Abstract

The Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT) signifies a pivotal shift in glacial–interglacial cycles with intensified interglacial warming, yet its underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Targeting the most sensitive component of oceanic heat uptake, the southern-sourced sub-surface waters, the post-MBT ocean heat dynamics are investigated using reconstructed deep and bottom thermocline temperatures from the Western Equatorial Pacific. Our results show that, since the MBT, the deep thermocline temperature has been gradually declining in association with cooling within the (sub)tropical Pacific upper ocean circulation. In contrast, the bottom thermocline temperature shows a pronounced rising trend independent of the calibration-derived uncertainties in its absolute estimates. Such post-MBT bottom thermocline warming is consistent with an enhanced advection of southern-sourced subsurface waters, as indicated by strengthened Southern Ocean meridional thermal gradients and concurrent warming in the southern subtropics. It is thus suggested that enhanced equatorward transport of southern-sourced subsurface waters, as a cross-hemispheric heat-redistribution pathway, may have elevated the background thermal state of post-MBT interglacials, highlighting the potential role of tropical-Southern Ocean connection in shaping climate trajectories.

---

## Introduction

The ocean stores more than 90% of the excess heat from anthropogenic forcing, making it the dominant reservoir of the present energy imbalance1–3. The way of the heat being partitioned within the thermocline and intermediate layers of the ocean influences energy exchange between hemispheres and hence climate feedbacks in modern days4–6, while paleo records show that meridional heat transport between the poles and the equator has influenced climate sensitivity on orbital to millennial timescales7–9. At the center of ocean heat redistribution is the Southern Ocean10–12, where formation and subduction of the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) and Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) ventilate the ocean interior with varying heat, carbon, and nutrients13–15. These water masses connect high-latitude surface forcing to low-latitude upper-ocean ventilation. Their past variability therefore provides key constraints on how ocean heat redistribution has shaped long-term climate transitions.

Modern observations highlight the importance of mode and intermediate waters in global heat uptake and reveal a strong hemispheric asymmetry3,16, with most ocean heat gain occurring in the Southern Hemisphere5. Yet instrumental records are too short to resolve their role over large-amplitude climate shifts. The Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT), occurring around ~430 thousand-years ago (ka), marks a fundamental shift toward warmer interglacials with higher atmospheric CO2, such as during the Holocene17,18. Although the MBT is not a direct analogue for modern warming, it provides a process-based reference for examining how internal reorganization of the climate system amplified interglacial warmth within the range of natural boundary conditions in the Quaternary (Figs. 1a, d, e). Given the relatively consistent orbital configurations over the past million years20, warmer interglacials after the MBT (post-MBT; ~430 ka onward) are generally attributed to stronger internal feedbacks than those before the MBT (~800–430 ka)19 (Figs. 1d, e), especially the processes of heat distribution within the ocean-atmosphere system.

Upper-ocean heat storage in the Pacific, shaped by wind-driven subtropical cells and thermocline dynamics, regulates the distribution of heat and moisture across the ocean-atmosphere system, thereby influencing global climate variability4,21,22. The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP) is a key region where the upper-ocean heat, coupling with intense atmospheric convection, modulates the ocean-atmosphere moisture budget on orbital time-scales8,23–25. Given such importance, the upper-ocean heat dynamics across the (sub)tropical Pacific is supposed to contribute to the post-MBT climate amplification. Previous studies have paid greater attention to deep-ocean ventilation26 and carbon cycling27, whereas the role of upper- to intermediate-ocean heat transport has been less explored. However, direct evidence linking variability in SAMW and AAIW formation to equatorward heat transport on orbital timescales remains limited.

Here we examine the changes in upper- to intermediate-ocean circulation through MBT, particularly involving SAMW and AAIW, to assess the associated effect of equatorward heat transport for post-MBT interglacial warming. To test this hypothesis, we reconstructed deep- and bottom-thermocline water temperatures (DTT and BTT, respectively) from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U148928 (2°07.19’N, 141°01.67’E, water depth 3421 m), located at the center of the IPWP, spanning the past ~670 kyr (Figs. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1a). The reconstructions are derived from Mg/Ca ratios of two planktonic foraminiferal species, Globorotalia tumida and Globorotalia crassaformis, which calcify at ~200 m (i.e., deep thermocline) and ~330–600 m (i.e., bottom thermocline)29–32, respectively (see Methods and Supplementary Material 1). Since available Mg/Ca-temperature calibrations for G. crassaformis were developed from Atlantic Ocean, all reported temperature variations focus on their relative variations and long-term trends that are little affected by the choice of calibrations32 (detailed in Supplementary Materials 1–3). The BTT variations are emphasized because of its direct linkage to the penetration depth and thermohaline properties of SAMW and AAIW, while the DTT record is used alongside to illustrate the thermocline dynamics across the MBT. By linking these changes in IPWP thermocline structure to southern-sourced intermediate-water circulation, we identified a mechanism of equatorward heat redistribution with implications for interglacial climate evolution.

---

## Results

Divergent deep and bottom thermocline changes

The DTT record of Site U1489 documents significant cycles with dominant 100-kyr and 23-kyr periodicities (above 90% confidence interval, Supplementary Figs. 2a, c), showing warmer values aligned with precession minima, especially during interglacial peaks (e.g., peaks at Marine Isotope Stages (MIS) 5, 9, 13, and 15; Figs. 1d, 2a; Supplementary Material 4). These patterns match with the shallower thermocline water temperature records from the IPWP and indicate a common modulation of precession-paced inter-hemispheric summer insolation gradient on the Pacific Subtropical Cells (STCs)8,21. Our results reaffirm a similar precession-driven STCs mechanism governing the thermal condition throughout the shallow to deep waters within the IPWP thermocline.

The mean values of our DTT show a slight cooling trend by ~0.9℃±0.2 ℃ (1σ, from 18.6 ℃ to 17.7 ℃) starting from ~470 ka, around the boundary between MIS 13 and 12 (Fig. 1b). This DTT cooling exhibits correspondence with the sea surface temperature (SST) trends in the center of the IPWP33,34 (Supplementary Figs. 3a, b) and with thermocline water temperature reconstructions across the western and eastern equatorial Pacific, pointing to a basin-wide shoaling and cooling of the tropical Pacific thermocline across the Pleistocene35,36(Supplementary Figs. 3c, d). Such changes were likely mediated by variations in the Equatorial Undercurrent and upwelling dynamics37,38.

The DTT cooling is further corroborated by a weak cooling trend in the mid-latitude North Pacific39, and a southward migration of both the Northern Hemisphere westerlies and the North Equatorial Counter Current during the same interval40,41(Figs. 2c, d), thus indicating a cooling and equatorward contraction of Pacific STCs (Fig. 2e). The associated cooling trend in the subtropical North Pacific would enhance thermocline ventilation along isopycnals21,42, thereby facilitating subduction of subtropical cold anomalies into the tropical upper-waters. Both modeling and observational studies indicate that temperature anomalies originating from the subtropics are transmitted equatorward to imprint on the equatorial thermocline, through pathways in the interior and western boundary of Pacific43,44. These lines of evidence allow us to attribute the long-term deep thermocline cooling in the Western Equatorial Pacific since ~470 ka to an intensified northern-sourced cold-water supply through a contracted STCs system. Independent reconstructions of G. tumida from the eastern tropical Pacific (ODP Site 1236) are consistent with our results and confirm the observed long-term DTT cooling as basin-scale thermocline changes rather than a site-specific feature or ecological artifacts45 (Supplementary Fig. 3e).

Differing from DTT, the BTT is dominated by obliquity cyclicities (41-kyr; Figs. 1c, e and Supplementary Figs. 2b, d), indicating sensitivity of the IPWP bottom thermocline to higher-latitude processes, which are more dominated by obliquity-paced cross-latitude insolation-gradient forcing46. Notably, variations in all the proxy records of G. crassaformis display relatively small amplitudes before MIS13 but enlarged variations after MIS12 (Supplementary Figs. 4e–g). The obliquity signal in BTT also strengthens since 400 ka and may be linked to the post-MBT intensification of obliquity forcing47, indicating an increased influence of higher-latitude processes on BTT variability.

Since the MBT, BTT rose on average by ~1.8±0.1 ℃ (1σ), from its prior-MBT foothold (from ~670 to 470 ka) with smaller-amplitude variations (~1 °C) (Fig. 1c). Sensitivity tests among Mg/Ca-temperature calibrations confirm the increase in G. crassaformis Mg/Ca ratios as the primary origin of such post-MBT BTT warming, and the choice of calibrations merely determines the baseline of absolute temperature estimates (Supplementary Material 3 and Supplementary Table 1). To explain the BTT warming trend since ~470 ka, one might speculate a long-term upward movement of the calcification depth of G. crassaformis. However, the δ13C of G. crassaformis closely parallels that of G. tumida and maintains a consistent offset from shallower-dwelling species (Supplementary Figs. 5a, b and Supplementary Material 4), indicating stable biogeochemical and thermohaline gradients vertically across their habitat depths. The δ18O of G. crassaformis do show a progressive negative shift, but it agrees largely with the BTT warming (Supplementary Figs. 4e, f). Moreover, given the consistent inter-species δ18O gradients from the mixed layer to the deep thermocline across the MBT, the progressive lightening of G. crassaformis δ18O may not be derived from a shoaling of its habitat depth but warming and/or freshening of the water-mass (Supplementary Figs. 5c–e). Collectively, the coherent trends since MIS 13/12 among the δ13C, δ18O, and the Mg/Ca-derived BTT at Site U1489, argue against any progressive habitat-depth shift of G. crassaformis, instead indicating changes in the thermohaline properties of the bottom-thermocline water mass.

Southern origin of the IPWP bottom thermocline warming

The substantial warming of bottom-thermocline waters in the center of the IPWP since ~470 ka (Fig. 3a) may be explained by two orthogonal scenarios: (1) vertically increased mixing from the shallower warmer waters, and (2) advectively from an enhanced equatorward transport of warmer waters via the SAMW and/or AAIW. The first scenario contradicts other proxy reconstructions. If downward mixing had dominated, the δ18O gradient between surface- and thermocline-dwelling foraminiferal species would have diminished. However, δ18O records from G. ruber, P. obliquiloculata, and G. tumida at Site U148948 varied parallel to one another, with little systematic change in the δ18O gradient between mixed layer and deep thermocline since ~670 ka (Supplementary Figs. 5c, e, and Supplementary Material 4). In addition, downward mixing would imply thickened warm-water pile-up in IPWP and thereby enlarged thermal contrast zonally across the tropical Pacific. However, the zonal SST gradient has slightly weakened since MIS12 (Fig. 2f), which conflicts with this scenario. Hence, a downward vertical mixing scenario is not supported by the available proxy evidence.

The second mechanism, advection of southern-sourced waters, is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. An increase of 2–4 ℃ in the SST gradients between the southern Subtropical Front (STF) and Subantarctic Front (SAF) since the MBT (Figs. 3a, c, d, Supplementary Fig. 6) is consistent with a strengthening of Southern Hemisphere westerlies (based on a conceptual estimate, see Supplementary Material 6) and supports a Southern Ocean source for the onset of the BTT warming. Stronger westerlies between the SAF and STF would deepen the mixed layer and enhance the Ekman pumping north of the SAF and thus strengthen the SAMW subduction49. Model experiments further suggest that poleward intensification of westerlies can more than double the rates of SAMW/AAIW subduction50,51. Proxy records from higher latitudes also show stronger subtropical flow of the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (ACC) across the Agulhas Plateau52, an intermediate-water cooling in the southwest Pacific associated with a poleward shift of the ACC53 (Fig. 3e), and intensified deep western boundary currents off New Zealand since ~450 ka54. Taken together, these observations indicate stronger subsurface water export from the sub-Antarctic zone and a more vigorous South Pacific overturning, supporting an intensified AAlW formation in accordance with the observed BTT warming.

After correcting for the temperature and ice-volume effects, the δ18O sw-ice of G. crassaformis still shows a trend toward more negative values (Supplementary Fig. 5d and Supplementary Material 5), likely reflecting an increase in buoyancy in its source water. Concurrently, SST in the southern Subtropical Front region has significantly increased since the MBT46 (Fig. 3c; Supplementary Fig. 7). Similar to modern warming scenarios55–57, warmer and shallower SAMW were likely produced with its subduction zone shifted poleward, due to warming-induced buoyancy increases58,59, thereby facilitating advection of the SAMW/AAIW along isopycnals into the IPWP bottom thermocline under strengthened westerlies. Modern observations also suggest that the equatorward heat transport in associated with Southern Ocean warming60, would be enhanced by intensified zonal flows61 and a deepened mixed layer north of the SAF62. Accordingly, together with an associated strengthening of the upper-layer circulation of the subtropical gyre63, the equatorward advection of the SAMW/AAIW has been further enhanced since the MBT.

It is noted that a “young, high-δ13C” signature in the bottom thermocline, as expected from well-ventilated Southern Ocean–sourced waters, is absent in our G. crassaformis record, largely due to the limitation of this δ13C tracer in this region64,65. This is mainly because, as SAMW and AAIW are transported northward, they experience mixing with subtropical and equatorial water masses64–66, and extensive biogeochemical modifications including remineralization of organic matters and transformations of inorganic carbon species67–70. These processes progressively attenuate the original δ13C signal. Consistent with this interpretation, such an expected “young, high-δ13C” signal can only be detected partially in some benthic δ13C records at mid-latitudes71, and may be further diminished equatorward into the tropical Pacific sub-surface.

In summary, the rise in BTT temperature since the MBT at Site U1489 coincided with SST warming in the Southern Hemisphere STF region and a strengthening of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies (Figs. 3a, c, d), suggesting a linkage to the source of bottom thermocline waters. Based on available evidence, we propose that enhanced subduction of a warmer SAMW, together with intensified AAIW advection and South Pacific overturning, facilitated transport of warmer waters from the subtropical Southern Ocean into the IPWP bottom thermocline.

Equatorward upper-ocean heat transport boosted warmer interglacials

The BTT and DTT records of Site U1489 suggest accelerated upper- to intermediate-ocean circulations towards the equator after the MBT. Consonantly, during the post-MBT interglacials, the southern trade winds may have been weakened, and the southern STF migrated southward, as supported by a warming in the Southern mid-latitudes and a reduced SST gradient between the southern subtropics and the IPWP72(Figs. 3b, c, and Supplementary Fig. 7). Also, an equatorward shift of northern westerly winds41 and a southward displacement of the IPWP since MIS12 (Fig. 3b) has been detected, in concert with our DTT cooling. These together indicate an inter-hemispheric asymmetry in Pacific upper-ocean circulation, which is supposed to have facilitated the heat uptake in southern mid-latitude Pacific, and strengthened the linkage between the IPWP and the Southern Ocean. It leads us to propose an enhanced heat storage in the Mode Waters during the post-MBT interglacial periods, in tandem with the elevated atmospheric pCO2 and orbital insolation heating26,73.

Since the MBT, the difference between our DTT and BTT decreased, while the δ18O sw-ice difference between G. tumida and G. crassaformis at Site U1489 increased (Figs. 4a, b, see Methods). These changes may reflect reduced thermal but enhanced salinity gradients between the two, which is consistent with an intensified AAIW subduction in the Southern Ocean since MIS13/12 (~470 ka) (Fig. 5). The relatively stable global deep-water temperatures74 (Fig. 4e), contrasted with warming in the mid- to high-latitude Southern Hemisphere53,75–79 (Figs. 3c and 4c, d), further support this interpretation. The sub-surface ocean circulation and heat export are often regarded as drivers of decadal variability in modern-climate studies4–6,80, whereas the high-latitude dynamics of AAIW and SRAMW in isolation have been largely examined by palaeoceanographic and observational studies14,81,82. By extending these perspectives from short-term variability to orbital timescales, our records suggest that Southern Ocean forcing operates within a dynamically coupled hemispheric heat-redistribution system, in which subsurface waters of the IPWP transmit high-latitude variability to the tropics. This equatorward subsurface transport increased tropical heat content and elevated the background thermal state, providing a key mechanism that could have contributed to the amplification of interglacial warmth after the MBT.

The proposed feedback that stronger Southern westerly winds intensify upper- to intermediate-ocean circulation and sustain northward ocean heat transport resonates with the observed post-industrial trends such as warming and expansion of subtropical western boundary currents55–57, increased Southern Ocean heat uptake10–12 and the strengthened pole-to-equator heat transport62. These insights provide specific targets for numerical model experiments, particularly sensitivity tests on the subduction rate and equatorward heat transport of SAMW/AAIW under varying climate scenarios. In any case, our findings underscore that Southern Ocean subsurface-water dynamics can effectively absorb the excess heat, and yield cascading effects on the tropical Pacific oceanic heat-structure and global climate state.

---

## Methods

Samples and Chronology

The studied cores from International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) Site U1489 (02°07.19ʹN, 141°01.67ʹE, 3421 m water depth) were drilled during Expedition 363 on the western slope of the southern Eauripik Rise, within the Caroline Basin north off Papua New Guinea28 (Supplementary Fig. 1a). A total of 332 sediment samples were collected from cores of the site at every ~5 cm interval from the upper 15.31 m core composite depth below seafloor (CCSF), covering the past ~670 kyr with a time resolution of ~2 kyr.

Site U1489 age model follows the published framework based on high-resolution Globigerinoides ruber δ18O48. A preliminary age model and baseline sedimentation rate were first defined using magnetic reversals from Hole D, owing to their consistency in depth scale. We aligned glacial–interglacial boundaries to the LR04 global benthic δ18O stack to define stratigraphic tie points and identify individual glacial cycles. These tie points were then used as age controls for constructing the age–depth model, with linear interpolation applied to all samples between 0 and 15.31 m. The resulting age model yields a relatively stable mean sedimentation rate of 2.1 ± 0.7 cm/kyr (1σ), generally higher during interglacials (1.0–4.0 cm/kyr; Supplementary Fig. 4a).

Subsurface Water Masses

In the western equatorial Pacific, shallow thermocline waters are ventilated from the subtropics through the Pacific Subtropical Cells (STCs)21,45 via the North and South Equatorial Currents83. While the Equatorial Undercurrent transports subsurface waters eastward across the basin, thereby linking hydrographic conditions between the western and eastern Pacific84. For the deeper part of the thermocline, the North Pacific Intermediate Water (NPIW) extends southward to ~8°N but is largely blocked from the equatorial band by the stronger influence of the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW)85. The latter is advected through the Solomon Sea along the north coast of Papua New Guinea and extends to ~15°N86–88, where it dominates the bottom thermocline of the western equatorial Pacific. The Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) forms north of the Subantarctic Front (SAF) by wintertime convection and is subsequently advected into the thermocline of the southern subtropical gyres as a key component of the upper limb of the Pacific overturning circulations14,89,90. The SAMW originates mainly from the east and central South Pacific, where it mixes with surrounding waters during formation and northward transport, often together with the AAIW, before entering the subtropical thermocline91,92 (Supplementary Fig. 1c).

At Site U1489, the Equatorial Pacific Intermediate Waters are mainly influenced by AAIW sourced from the southeast Pacific, with additional contributions from the Coral and Tasman Seas and direct Southern Ocean inflow64,65. These circulation pathways make Site U1489 particularly suitable for reconstructing thermocline- and intermediate-water variations and their associated interactions between high and low latitudes. Consistent with previous studies93,94, the GLODAP δ13C distribution shows that newly subducted AAIWP and SAMW exhibit relatively high δ13C values, reflecting quick ventilations from the air-sea interface95 (Supplementary Fig. 1d). In contrast, the deep and bottom thermocline in the western Pacific warm pool have lower δ13C, indicating the attenuation of source water signals due to addition of respired carbon and mixing with older waters.

Planktonic foraminiferal proxies

The subsurface-dwelling species Globorotalia tumida, which calcifies at ~200 m in the western equatorial Pacific29 (detailed in Supplementary Material 1), is commonly used as an indicator of deep thermocline conditions36,96,97. Globorotalia crassaformis calcifies at ~330–600 m in the tropical ocean30,31, and generally above the intermediate waters across ocean basins30–32, so it has been extensively applied to reconstruct deepest thermocline/intermediate-water properties in both the Pacific and Atlantic since the Pliocene30–32,98. Accordingly, we use G. tumida as a proxy for the deep thermocline and G. crassaformis as a proxy for the bottom thermocline, defined relative to their calcification depths (Supplementary Material 1). Proxy records from these species, together with sea surface temperature anomaly (SSTA) stacks (detailed in Supplementary Material 6), therefore provide a means to examine connections between the Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP), Pacific STCs, and Southern Hemisphere mid-latitude processes mediated by the AAIW and SAMW.

Stable isotope and Mg/Ca-temperature analyses

Between 25 and 30 well-preserved specimens of G. tumida and G. crassaformis were hand-picked from the 355–425 μm and 250–425 μm size fractions for stable isotope and Mg/Ca measurement, respectively. All specimens are well preserved based on scanning electron microscopy examinations (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary Material 2).

Stable isotope analyses were conducted on a Finnigan MAT253 mass spectrometer with a Kiel IV carbonate preparation device at State Key Laboratory of Marine Geology, Tongji University, following ref. 99. Long-term measurement standard deviation is 0.07‰ for δ18O and 0.05‰ (1σ) for δ13C. Results were calibrated to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) scale using the NBS19 standard. The average sampling resolution is ~2–3 kyr for both isotope and Mg/Ca records.

For Mg/Ca analyses, we used a composite cleaning protocol based on the established procedures100 with steps of silicate removal101 and reductive cleaning102. The protocol included sequential removal of clays, oxidative and reductive cleaning, weak acid leaching, and multiple rinses with ultrapure water to eliminate detrital clays, Fe–Mn oxides, and organic matter. Mg/Ca ratios were measured on an Agilent 5110 inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) at the Marine Elements Analysis Laboratory, Northwest University, China. Instrumental drift and analytical precision were monitored using ECRM 752-159103, analyzed after every 11 samples. Replicate analyses (n = 30) yielded reproducibility of 5.1% for G. tumida and 3.2% for G. crassaformis.

Cleaning effectiveness was assessed by correlations between Mg/Ca and Al/Ca, Fe/Ca, and Mn/Ca ratios (Supplementary Figs. 9a–h). In G. tumida, a weak positive correlation between Mn/Ca and Mg/Ca was detected (R2 = 0.26). In contrast, Mn/Ca and Mg/Ca of G. crassaformis shows a strong correlation (R2=0.74, Supplementary Figs. 9i–n), primarily due to elevated Mn/Ca values after ~270 ka (Supplementary Fig. 9f), with no apparent link to BTT warming. This relationship, consistent with previous reports of Mn–Mg coupling104–106, is attributed to Mn-rich surface coatings. Following ref. 107, a Mn correction (assuming Mg/Mn = 0.2 mmol/mol) was applied.

Because Site U1489 lies at a depth of ~3421 m, both dissolution and Mn-corrections were applied following refs. 107 and 108. The Mg/Ca ratio in G. tumida was then converted to deep thermocline temperature (DTT) using a species-specific calibration for the 355–425 μm size fraction from western equatorial Pacific29 (Mg/Ca = 0.33exp (0.097 × DTT)). This calibration was selected after evaluating results from alternative equations against modern hydrographic data (Supplementary Figs. 1b, 10a, 11a–d; see Supplementary Material 3 for details). For G. crassaformis, specific calibration for the western equatorial Pacific has not been established. The Atlantic-based calibration, Mg/Ca = 0.658exp (0.122 × BTT)32 with corrections for Mn-contamination and dissolution108,109, gives the most reasonable BTT estimates, in terms of the comparable Late-Holocene BTT values with respect to the modern temperatures at 330–600 m depth in the western equatorial Pacific (Supplementary Figs. 1b, S10b, 11e–h). Uncertainties were calculated following ref. 109, yielding mean errors of 1.7 ℃ for DTT and 0.6 ℃ for BTT (1σ), respectively.

Calculation of seawater δ18O

Seawater δ18O (δ18Osw) was calculated using the equation from ref. 110: δ18Osw (VSMOW, ‰) = (T(°C) -16.5+4.8×δ18Ocalcite(VPDB, ‰))/4.8+0.27. The global ice volume effect, as reported by ref. 111 was then removed to obtain δ18Osw-ice, which reflects local/regional freshwater (or salinity) budget. The δ18Osw-ice errors (see ref. 109 for details) are 0.03‰ for G. tumida and 0.10‰ for G. crassaformis (1σ).

Regional SST stacks and gradients

We compiled subsurface/thermocline records from the IODP Site U1489 and SST reconstructions from Western and Eastern Equatorial Pacific, and Southern Ocean frontal zones (STF and SAF). All datasets, proxies (Mg/Ca or alkenone), coordinates, water depths, and references are listed in Supplementary Table 2. For regional stacks, individual series were linearly interpolated to 4-kyr, adjusted by subtracting the maximum value over the entire time window, smoothed with a 20-kyr running mean, and then averaged. When combining Mg/Ca and alkenone, we used anomalies to minimize method-specific offsets (detailed discussion see Supplementary Material 6). Zonal equatorial Pacific SST gradient is calculated by the difference of SST anomaly between western and eastern equatorial Pacific (ΔSSTAW−E = SSSTAMD97-2140 − SSTODP846), and meridional frontal gradient by those between STF and SAF (ΔSSTASTF−SAF = SST stack (STF) − SST stack (SAF); detailed in Supplementary Material 7).

Time series analyses

To evaluate the orbital pacing and long-term trends, all SSTA records shown in the main text were first linearly interpolated at 4-kyr intervals, and then smoothed with a 20-kyr running average after. Records from IODP Site U1489 were processed using a three-point running average and LOESS smoothing with a Gaussian fit (span = 0.5), and then further smoothed with LOESS (smoothing factor = 0.3) to acquire their long-term trends. Spectral analysis was carried out using the REDFIT procedure112 as implemented in PAST v4.03113. Rectangular windows were applied with an oversampling factor of 6, and the data were divided into two equal-length segments to estimate the red-noise spectra. Wavelet analysis of the temperature reconstructions was performed using Acycle v2.8, following standard procedures114. RAMPFIT regressions were applied to identify changing points in long-term trends115.

Based on high-resolution paleoceanographic reconstructions of deep and bottom thermocline temperatures from Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP) records, Yang et al. investigate the thermal evolution of the upper-to-intermediate ocean equatorial Pacific over the last 700 ka. The central discussion is based on the differences in behavior between two thermocline depths after ~470 ka, where small deep thermocline cooling is concomitant with substantial warming of bottom thermocline temperatures. Authors argue that this warming originates from the Southern Ocean, driven by Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) with intensification of Antarctic Intermediate Water formation. Overall, the paper is really good. Although disagreements among compared records could be better accounted for to avoid simplification of the mechanism, the discussion is well-written and presents a plausible mechanism, is conclusive, providing novel insights into thermal evolution and ocean-atmospheric interactions in the southern Pacific across the Mid-Brunhes Transition (MBT). The new dataset is valuable, and, together with the interpretations, it makes a significant contribution to the scientific community. Additionally, there are a few major points that need to be improved to adhere to a global framework and to clarify data comparisons with existing published records.
